quote: braischen Function durch Congruenzen nach Modulsystemen aus? Indem also an Stelle der Entwicklungen nach gebrochnen Potenzen Congruenzbedingungen treten.
english: ...[how does one express ... of the alge]braic function of several variables through congruences with respect to module systems? So that congruence conditions take the place of expansions in fractional powers.
topic: The page ends a question about expressing algebraic functions of several variables and maxima-minima conditions through congruences with respect to module systems, then states and begins proving a theorem that a continuous function uniformly approximated by rational functions which approximately satisfy a rational differential relation is differentiable and satisfies the differential equation F = 0.

triage.modern_statement: The fragment's opening is cut off, so we can't see exactly which property of the algebraic function Hilbert meant. Most likely it is the local behaviour at singular points (branching), possibly together with the maxima-minima conditions mentioned on the page. In modern terms, the question seems to be: can the local conditions on algebraic functions or varieties in several variables, which were classically stated through Puiseux expansions in fractional powers, be restated purely in terms of ideals (Hilbert's 'module systems')? That would mean stating them as membership conditions in ideals or local primary components ('congruences modulo an ideal') instead of as series expansions.
triage.answered_by: This was not answered as a single named theorem. It was a research program, and later work carried it out. Max Noether's fundamental theorem (AF+BG, 1873) expresses a curve's passing through intersection points as a local ideal-membership condition. Lasker, Macaulay and Emmy Noether's primary-decomposition ideal theory (1905 to 1920s) generalized this. Zariski's algebraic, valuation-theoretic theory of singularities (1930s to 1940s) took the place of Puiseux expansions. Separately, the Jung–Abhyankar theorem covers Puiseux expansions in several variables for quasi-ordinary singularities. Whether any of these authors were responding to this diary note is not documented.

evidence.claim: Max Noether's AF+BG theorem says that if a curve's equation lies locally, at each intersection point, in the ideal generated by F and G, then it lies in the global ideal. This is a local condition stated as ideal membership, i.e. a congruence modulo a module system.
The Noether fundamental theorem combines a global condition with local conditions at the intersection points.
Macaulay's work places the Lasker–Noether theorem as the most general and fundamental ideal-theoretic result in this line, growing out of Max Noether's theory.
Zariski rebuilt the theory of singularities and resolution algebraically, using valuation and ideal theory.
Valuation-theoretic local uniformization at singular points is still being developed. Teissier's work does this partly by generalizing what is done for plane branches.

The Abhyankar–Jung theorem: roots of quasi-ordinary polynomials are Puiseux power series in several variables. This covers the case where fractional-power expansions do still work in several variables.

triage.why: The note is a programmatic question: replace Puiseux (fractional-power) expansions with congruence conditions modulo ideals. This matches the historical path from Noether's local conditions to Lasker–Noether–Macaulay ideal theory and Zariski's algebraic theory of singularities. That line of work did largely carry out such a program, and valuation theory and local uniformization are still active research areas. However, the start of the sentence is missing, so the exact object to be expressed is unknown. It is not among Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. No source links this diary entry to any specific later result, so the identification is interpretive and could also reasonably be judged too fragmentary.
